name: bluewater-15-they-gave-her-until-friday
lines: Thursday. Nine in the morning. A text from a number she doesn't know.
It says, I've been paid to post twenty bad reviews on your business. Pay me, and I won't.
She thinks it's spam. She deletes it.
By lunch, her four point nine is a four point one.
This is the nastiest scam aimed at small businesses right now. And most owners make it worse.
Meet Nora. She's a made up example. Eleven years moving families across town. Two trucks. Three hundred and twelve reviews.
Every one of them earned. One couch at a time.
The scam, though, is real. News stations across the US have been covering it all year.
One watchdog has tracked more than a hundred and fifty businesses hit the same way.
How the trap works.
It starts with a flood. Ten, twenty one star reviews in a few hours.
From people she never moved. Names she's never seen.
And they're detailed. Broken dishes. A scratched piano. Movers who never showed.
Then comes the second message. A price. And a promise that it all goes away.
In cases one watchdog looked at, the messages came from foreign phone numbers.
And it works, because nobody reads three hundred reviews. They read the number at the top.
The two mistakes.
Nora did what almost everyone does. Mistake one. She wrote back.
Who are you? Who paid you? Take them down, or I'm calling the police.
Now he knows three things. The number is real. The owner is scared. And she reads her messages.
The price went up.
Mistake two came at eleven that night. She opened her banking app.
It's only a few hundred dollars. Say three hundred. And the reviews would be gone by morning.
Here's what Google itself says about that. Paying can encourage more attempts, and it doesn't guarantee the reviews come down.
You'd be paying a stranger to learn that you pay.
Eleven p.m.
Her thumb was on the send button.
Her brother Leo drives the second truck. He looked over her shoulder, and said one thing.
Don't pay him. Screenshot him.
Because the scammer had made one mistake. He put it in writing.
The fake reviews look like opinions. The message is a ransom note.
And Google has a form built for exactly that.
What to do instead.
Here's the playbook. Five moves. None of them cost a dollar.
One. Don't answer, and don't pay. Not a word. Not a cent.
Two. Screenshot everything. The message, the number, the date, the price.
Three. Copy the link to every fake review, and write down when the flood began.
Four. Send it all through Google's merchant extortion report form. It's on the Business Profile help site.
Google says its team investigates, and tells you the outcome.
Some owners have reported the fakes gone within a day. Not everyone. Not always fast.
Five. While you wait, answer the fakes in public. Calm. Short. Written for the next customer reading.
We have no record of this customer. We've reported this review to Google as part of an extortion attempt.
A stranger reading that doesn't see a bad mover. They see an owner under attack, who kept her head.
And then do the one thing the scammer can't. Ask your real customers.
Every family you moved this month. One text. How did we do?
Twenty fakes are loud next to thirty real reviews. Next to three hundred, they're a bad afternoon.
Now the honest part. Nobody can promise how fast Google moves, or that every fake comes down.
And the form only covers one thing. Somebody demanding money or favors to remove reviews.
A real unhappy customer is a different problem. You answer that one. You don't report it.
Friday. The deadline he gave her.
Nora didn't pay. She sent the form on Thursday night, and went to bed angry.
In our story, the fakes came down the following week. Yours might take longer.
The text thread is still on her phone. Unanswered.
They're counting on you being scared and fast.
Be calm. Be slow. Keep the receipts.
Your reputation took eleven years. Don't hand it to a stranger for three hundred dollars.
If you want your marketing handled by people who play it straight, that's us. Bluewater Co dot C A.
